entries.definition: Artificial intelligence that creates new content, such as text, images or program code, from a prompt, using patterns learned from training data.
A design tool that plans an object in three sections: Name, Properties/Attributes and Methods.
A three-column table summarising one task: its inputs, the processes that turn them into results, and its outputs.
Text: character and string. Numeric: integer, floating point and date/time. And Boolean.
A text data type that holds exactly one letter, digit or symbol; a string holds a sequence of them.
A list of values of a single data type under one name, each reached by one integer index.
Values of one data type arranged in rows and columns, each reached by a row index and a column index.
A data structure that groups related values of varying data types under one name, each stored in its own field.
Data that comes into a solution from an outside file or system: unstructured (plain text) or structured (delimited or XML).
A structured text file that stores each value between named tags in a hierarchy: self-describing, extensible and portable between systems.
An OOP principle: a class hides the details of how it works and exposes only what other code needs.
An OOP principle: a class keeps attributes with the methods that work on them, and stops other code reaching those attributes directly.
An OOP principle: features shared by two or more classes are moved up into a more general superclass they inherit from.
An OOP principle: a subclass automatically receives its superclass's attributes and methods, and can add its own or override them.
A template that defines the attributes and methods shared by every object of one type.
A single instance made from a class while the program runs, holding its own attribute values.
The code structures that determine how an algorithm behaves: sequence, selection (branching) and repetition (iteration).
A variable declared inside a function or method: usable anywhere in that module but nowhere else, and only while the module runs.
A variable declared outside every module, so any part of the program can read or change it while the program runs.
Guidelines that keep the names given to parts of a solution consistent, making its code quicker and easier to read and understand.
A naming convention that starts each name with a short prefix showing its data type or control type, as in intAge or btnSave.
A naming convention that joins words without spaces, the first in lower case and each later word capitalised, as in totalCost.
A naming convention that writes every word in lower case with an underscore between words, as in total_cost.
Checking, by hand or electronically, that data is reasonable and complete, as it is input or after it has been stored.
Existence (a required field isn't blank), type (the expected data type) and range (within set limits).
Comments in the source code that explain and justify its data and code structures, support maintenance and mark stubs for future development.
Checks each element in turn from the first until it finds the target or reaches the end; works on unsorted data.
Compares the target with the middle of sorted data and discards the half that can't hold it, until found or none remain.
On each pass, finds the smallest value in the unsorted part and swaps it into the next position of the sorted part.
Chooses a pivot, partitions the list into smaller values before it and larger values after, then sorts each part the same way.
Problems that stop a program working as expected, classed as syntax, logic or run-time.
Code that breaks the language's rules, such as a missing bracket, so it can't be compiled and run.
A mistake that makes a program give incorrect output, such as a wrong calculation, while it still runs without crashing.
Divide by zero, index out of range, overflow and type mismatch: failures while a program runs that crash it unless handled.
Finding the errors already in code, fixing them, then testing that the changes work, during development as the code is written.
A table with one row per test case: the test number, each input, the expected output and the actual output.

entries.term: The four reasons for a software project
entries.definition: Reducing costs, increasing productivity and efficiency, addressing gaps in the market, and meeting organisational objectives or needs.
A short document at a project's start outlining the problem, need or opportunity, proposed users, programming languages, feasibility and originality.
A detailed proposal for how a project will be managed: its tasks, their sequence and time, dependencies, milestones and the critical path.
A chart showing each task as a bar on a timeline, with dependencies, milestones and the critical path, updated to monitor progress.
A link between two tasks in which one can't start until the other, its predecessor, has finished.
A significant point in a project, such as the end of a PSM stage, with no duration, used to check progress.
The longest chain of dependent tasks from start to finish; its length is the shortest time the project can take.
Data that researchers gather themselves, straight from its sources, such as through surveys, interviews or observations; raw and unprocessed.
Data that someone other than the researcher has already collected, summarised or analysed, such as reports, articles and data sets.
Interviews (a few people, in depth), surveys (many people, quickly), observations (how a task is really done) and reports (existing records).
A requirement that states something the solution must do: accept inputs, produce outputs or carry out a function such as validating data.
A requirement describing a quality the solution must have, such as usability, reliability, portability, robustness or maintainability.
A limit the solution must be designed within: economic (cost and time), technical, social (users' expertise), legal or usability.
The boundaries of a solution or version: what it will address and what it will not.
A Level 0 diagram showing the whole system as one circle, exchanging labelled data flows with external entities drawn as rectangles.
A Level 1 diagram of how data moves between external entities, processes and data stores; entities and stores never connect directly.
A UML diagram of how users interact with a system: actors outside a boundary, use cases inside, joined by associations.
The role of a user who interacts with a system to achieve a goal, drawn as a stick figure; never an organisation or device.
Joins a base use case to shared behaviour that runs every time the base runs; the arrow points from the base.
Joins an optional addition, run only under a condition, to a base use case; the arrow points to the base.
A document describing what a software solution is intended to do and its environment: requirements, scope, constraints, technical environments and user characteristics.
The main laws that people, businesses and government bodies must obey when using intellectual property or collecting and holding private data.
Copying data and keeping the copy apart from the original, so it can be restored if the data is lost.
Full (everything), differential (changes since the last full copy) and incremental (changes since the last copy of any kind).
A process of coming up with ideas and building on them, cycling from a first concept through to a developed design.
Annotations, brainstorming, mind maps, mood boards and sketches.
A diagram that organises ideas around a central theme, with main ideas branching out into more specific ones.
Using critical and creative thought to come up with and judge new ideas, then defining the preferred solution precisely enough to build.
The time, cost and effort it takes to achieve the intended results: the less it takes, the better.
How well a solution, design, security strategy or development practice works, and how far it achieves what it was meant to do.
Specific, measurable checks drawn from the requirements, used to choose a design idea and later to judge the finished solution.
English-like statements, written in order, that represent an algorithm for solving a problem.
A table that plans the data a module needs, giving each item at least a name and a data type.
Taking into account how users perceive a digital system and how they react as they interact with it.
Usability, security (authentication and data protection), interoperability and affordance.
How clearly an interface element's appearance shows what it does and how to use it, like a button that looks pressable.
How easily the intended users can learn and operate a solution to complete their tasks, including ease of use and accessibility.
Recognised qualities that help a solution work well, be easy to use and look good, grouped under functionality, usability and appearance.
A design principle: making elements clearly different in colour, size, weight or shape, so important items stand out and text is readable.
Developing a solution with its actual users taking part at every stage, such as interviews, design feedback and beta testing.
Code with meaningful names, consistent indenting and no repeated or unneeded lines, so it takes less effort to read, change and test.
An array in which every element is a record with the same fields, suiting many items with fields of different types.
A keyword written before an attribute or method that sets which code may use it.
Lets any code in the program use the attribute or method.
Limits an attribute or method to the class's own methods and its subclasses.
Limits an attribute or method to the class's own methods only.
A shared store for a project's code and the full history of changes to it, supporting version control and teamwork.
A defined interface through which separate programs communicate, exchanging data or services without knowing how the other works inside.
Ready-made code, such as functions and classes, packaged so developers can call it for common tasks rather than writing it themselves.
A development tool that generates or suggests code as the developer works and can automate debugging and testing.
A marker on a line of code that pauses execution there, so variable values can be inspected and the code stepped through.
Input values chosen to check that a module works: valid, invalid and boundary values, each with its expected output.
One planned test: particular input values and the output the requirements say should result.
Testing throughout development that modules or the whole solution meet every requirement and work as intended, by the developers themselves, independent testers or high-level users.
Testing in which intended user groups try a solution, checking it meets every requirement, works as expected, is stable and is usable.
Constructing a testing plan and test scenarios, observing users as they work through them, and documenting the results.
A realistic task, described in the user's own terms, that a tester carries out; it states the goal, not the steps.
A plan for judging how well an implemented solution meets its requirements: the evaluation criteria, the time frame and who is responsible.
Applying the evaluation criteria to the data collected, to judge how efficiently and effectively the solution meets its requirements.

entries.term: The three factors that affect a project plan
entries.definition: Personnel changes, scope creep and technical issues.
The gradual, uncontrolled growth of a project's features or requirements after its scope is agreed, usually without extra time or budget.
Someone leaves, joins or is moved to other work, so tasks are delayed or reassigned and knowledge may be lost.
Problems with hardware, software or tools, such as a failed server or a changed API, that add unplanned work.

entries.term: The three ways to record a project's progress
entries.definition: Adjustments to tasks and time frames, annotations to the project plan, and logs or journals.
A note on the plan recording what happened, why, and its effect.
A change made to the plan in response to what happened: to a time frame or to a task.
A dated record of the tasks worked on, problems met, decisions made and changes to the plan, written at the time.
Looking back at how many changes the plan needed, why each was necessary, and how they affected completing the project.
A broad, long-term aim stating what an organisation wants to achieve; it usually can't be measured directly.
A specific, measurable target with a time frame, set to help an organisation achieve one of its goals.
Software designed, built and maintained by the organisation's own employees, using its own equipment and processes.
Software designed and built for the organisation by another company or a contractor, under a contract setting requirements, cost and deadline.
A broad field bringing together digital systems, how organisations operate, threats to data and systems, legal and ethical issues, and managing risk.
Actions, devices or events that could compromise the security or integrity of data and information: accidental, deliberate or events-based.
A weakness in a system, program, process or development environment that a threat could exploit to cause harm.
The chance that a threat will exploit a vulnerability, considered together with how much harm it would cause.
A threat from someone with legitimate access, such as an employee or contractor, whose action could harm systems, code or data.
A vulnerability where development, testing and production share one environment, so one faulty change can corrupt real data or take the live system down.
Measures that help protect individuals, systems, networks, organisations and data: hardware, software, physical equipment, procedures or electronic measures.

entries.term: The six security controls for software development
entries.definition: Code review, encryption, robust identity and access management, regular updates and patches, separated environments, and version control with code repositories.
Recording every change to code with who made it and when, so changes can be traced and rolled back; not a backup.
The process of making sure each member of an organisation can reach only the data, modules and systems their assigned duties need.
Turning data and information from plain text into a coded form, to keep it from being compromised.
The method that uses one key both to encrypt and to decrypt.
The method that uses a public key to encrypt and a matching private key to decrypt.
A second developer examines code before it is merged, catching vulnerabilities the author missed.
Keeping development, testing and production apart, so unfinished code can't affect the live system and developers don't need live data.
The principle that each user, program or process gets only the access rights its duties require.
A structured way of finding and dealing with the security threats to a system, begun during design and revisited whenever it changes.
Defining security requirements, identifying and mitigating threats, and confirming the threats have been mitigated.
The security controls in place, exposure to vulnerabilities and risks, and legal compliance.

entries.term: Effectiveness measures for a security strategy
entries.definition: Confidentiality, integrity and availability.
Guidelines written so organisations and governments apply strategies that keep data and information secure across networks and uphold the highest ethical standards.
A prioritised set of eight mitigation strategies from the Australian Cyber Security Centre, such as patching, multi-factor authentication and regular backups.
A cyber security framework from the Australian Cyber Security Centre setting out principles and detailed controls, including guidelines for software development.
Commonwealth law giving the owner of an original work, including program code, exclusive rights to copy, adapt, publish and share it.
Commonwealth law on how Australian Government agencies and many private organisations handle personal information, through the Australian Privacy Principles.
Victorian law on how public sector bodies, such as departments and councils, handle personal information, through the Information Privacy Principles.
Situations that call moral standards, principles or expectations into question, and that can affect individuals, organisations or both.

entries.term: The ethical issues in software development
entries.definition: Intellectual property and copyright issues, ineffective security practices, and the use of AI during development.

entries.term: Strategies for improving secure development practices
entries.definition: Onboarding or induction and developer training focused on secure development, and developing risk management plans.
Lists the potential risks to a project, rates each one's likelihood and impact, and proposes security controls to reduce them.

entries.term: The four stages of the PSM
entries.definition: Analysis, design, development and evaluation, in that order.
Works out what the solution must do and the conditions it must work within: requirements, constraints and scope.
Plans how the solution will work and look before any code is written, and develops the evaluation criteria.
Builds the solution from the requirements and designs: coding it, validating its input, testing and debugging it, and documenting it.
Judges how well the finished solution meets its requirements once it has been developed and put into use.
Solution requirements, solution constraints and solution scope.
Solution design and evaluation criteria.
Manipulation (coding), validation, testing and documentation.
Evaluation strategy and solution evaluation.
The development activity of coding the solution with suitable algorithms and features of the programming language.
Recognising where computation applies to a problem and reasoning about it in logical, algorithmic, recursive and inferential ways.
Using a variety of techniques to develop ideas and designs, including forming, analysing and judging the questions asked, data used and decisions made.
An approach that looks at the whole picture, analysing how an information system's data, processes, people and digital systems interact.
The hardware, software and other elements, and how they are interconnected, used to build digital solutions.
Generally agreed approaches to using digital systems or representing data, followed so a solution stays consistent throughout.
How data and information physically look when presented, for example as images, graphs, tables, text or web pages.
How sound data is overall, judged by its accuracy, authenticity, correctness, reasonableness, relevance and timeliness.
Checking that data is accurate and consistent, for example by proofreading it or comparing it with other sources.
Moving data that is rarely needed out of a working system into storage accessed less often, kept for later use or because rules require it.
Methods and software that let organisations collect data, correct it, analyse it for patterns, trends and relationships, and present the findings visually.
Measures that summarise a data set: central tendency (average, median) and variability and spread (such as range and standard deviation).
Using software to present analysed data graphically, as charts, graphs, maps and diagrams, helping users explore large amounts of data for patterns.
Graphical displays of data that users can explore interactively, where the data shown can change through interaction or as live data is added.
A single visual that gives an overview of a topic by bringing complex data or information together, so patterns show at a glance.
